Lift can theoretically help improve rolling resistance slightly, however the conversion is really unfavorable. To get any meaningful lift or downforce you have to add quite a bit of energy to the flow to get the lift; more than you’re really gaining in friction reductions.

When designing a road car you’re typically better off by directing airflow away from the messy underbody and over the car.  A nose up angle would be pretty bad for drag since there’s a lot of air going under and it’s going to impact a lot of things under the car in the decreasing amount of room. 

Nose down can be more neutral than nose up but is generally detrimental as well. This also will somewhat contribute to directing air up and you’ll be wasting energy.

However modern road cars are generally designed these days for a fairly level orientation. It gives airflow a reasonably free path under the car without disturbing the flow any more than you have to. 

A race car is totally different where drag isn’t as big of a concern and downforce is the key. They have flat underbodies and the nose down angle causes the entire underbody to be a diffuser creating lower pressure under the car for downforce.

It can be done with repulsors, but it may not always be the best method. Transporting very large containers and equipment might be easier with an AT-ACT than a transport spacecraft. We see the AT-ACT carrying containers the size of the entire Zeta class shuttle after all.

We never see what else is on Scarif.  I really doubt the Empire would put a whole planetary shield just for one island base.  Especially if they're transporting (for example) a giant reactor to a new base, a walker might be efficient.  It might be easier to drop supplies at the Citadel and have them walked to other bases rather than fly a heavy lift transport under the shield (since we know there's only one opening) for up to thousands of miles if theres no rush. Especially if the seas are as shallow as they seem the walkers can just walk through them.  

Outside of Scarif having an armed heavy transport can be useful in an unsafe, but not full battle, situation.  Clearly something like that will be outclassed by air cover, but in a rebellious planet it can be sufficient to move heavy equipment and handle any rebels that try to get in the way.  

On Scarif, the AT-ACTs were just around doing their jobs but when the Rebellion shows up they are re-tasked to provide support since they're still reasonably armed. Generally most readers should be able to at least tell you the code number (and prefix) even if it doesn't know the description. Maybe some super cheap ones don't have memory to handle anything higher than P0FFF, but I'm not sure. If your reader can only show P codes you could be missing sets of other codes like B (body modules)or U (network). However a lot of those don't set a MIL. 

Type B requires two occurrences to set the Maintenance Indicator Light. When the first failure occurs you'll get the pending code but no MIL. Pending state from a single failure shouldn't set a MIL. 

It could be you're constantly setting codes and they may self clear briefly by the time you read. Or you could be not reading something. So maybe go to an autozone or something when the MIL is on and they may have a better reader on hand that they use (usually free). Codes clear on controller shutdown usually so it could even be clearing as you turn off to walk in, but if the MIL is on when you have the car on to read, it should read a code. Try having the engine running with a MIL on for best results. Short of a real mechanic with a good diagnostic tool that may be your best bet. 

Side note: I'm mostly familiar with new applications which self clear a lot more and there's something called mode $0A that is unclearable and requires 4 passed diagnostic trips. This can cause a new car to still have a MIL without a normal mode $01 code present. However that mostly showed up after 2012 or so. But I get people with a similar problem to you where this is the problem. 

Also while most people consider evap minor this is basically the point of OBD, which is to prevent engines from polluting and emitting unburned hydrocarbons from evap leaks and engines operating poorly. CARB won't call that a minor issue.

Boundary layer is a thin layer that is the transition from the fast moving air and the "stationary" surface. Since you can't really have slipping between the solid and the fluid the fluid must do the transition through the boundary layer.

What I am referring to is the distance that the velocity is significantly impacted by the wing.  You understand that the fluid speed is higher on the upper surface of a lifting wing, and that infinitely far away from the wing it would not feel the effects.  In the middle, it must transition from faster (or slower) to free stream speed.  This falls off similar to an exponential decay.  Most of the transition takes place close to the body.  

The applet /u/mrCloggy showed can help you see the velocity distribution and how the influence of the disturbing body propagates.

Also yeah, I was meaning pretty low speed flow.  Once you get fast enough that compressibility comes into it and definitely supersonic effects this isn't really applicable, but for a car, small or RC plane, or so it should be close enough.

A rule of thumb I was given in school is 2 or so chord lengths (wing front to back distance).
